subject: Chemistry
title: Imatinib: The First Targeted Cancer Drug
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Imatinib: The First Targeted Cancer Drug.

hook.text: Imatinib turned chronic myeloid leukemia from a death sentence into a manageable disease. It was the first precision cancer drug.

buildup.text: CML is caused by one mutation: the Philadelphia chromosome creates a faulty protein (BCR-ABL) that tells cells to divide forever.

discovery.text: Imatinib was designed to fit precisely into the BCR-ABL protein's active site, blocking it like a key jammed in a lock.

twist.text: Before imatinib, CML patients survived 3-5 years. With it, survival is near-normal lifespan—one pill daily controls the disease.

climax.text: Imatinib proved that understanding a cancer's specific chemistry lets you design a precise weapon against it.

punchline.text: One mutation, one drug, one target. Precision medicine's first triumph.

quiz.question: What makes imatinib different from traditional chemotherapy?
options: It targets only the specific mutant protein causing the cancer, sparing healthy cells
It kills all rapidly dividing cells in the body
It strengthens the immune system to fight cancer naturally

details.summary: Imatinib was designed to specifically inhibit the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase, a fusion protein caused by the Philadelphia chromosome translocation that drives chronic myeloid leukemia. It transformed CML from a rapidly fatal disease to a manageable condition with over 90 percent five-year survival.
details.whyItMatters: Imatinib proved that understanding the molecular cause of a specific cancer could lead to a precisely targeted drug. It became the model for all subsequent targeted cancer therapies and precision medicine.
takeaways: Imatinib specifically blocks the BCR-ABL fusion protein in CML cells
It transformed CML five-year survival from 30 to over 90 percent
It established the paradigm of targeted therapy based on molecular cause

faq.question: How does targeting a specific protein reduce side effects compared to chemotherapy?
faq.answer: Traditional chemotherapy kills all rapidly dividing cells, damaging healthy tissues. Imatinib targets only the BCR-ABL protein that is unique to CML cells. Normal cells lack this protein and are largely unaffected. This selectivity dramatically reduces the severe side effects of treatment.

faq.question: Can cancer cells develop resistance to imatinib?
faq.answer: Yes. Mutations in the BCR-ABL kinase domain can alter the drug binding site, preventing imatinib from attaching. Second and third-generation inhibitors like dasatinib and ponatinib were developed to overcome common resistance mutations, staying ahead of cancer's evolutionary adaptations.
